text: The applicant was born in 1992.
The applicant lives in St Petersburg.
The applicant was represented by Ms K. Mikhaylova, a lawyer practising in St Petersburg.
The Government were represented by Mr M. Galperin, the Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights.
The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.
On 27 September 2013 a group of LGBTI rights activists informed the St Petersburg authorities of their intention to hold a meeting to mark Coming Out Day (an annual LGBTI awareness day).
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: The meeting to mark Coming Out Day was planned to take place from 2 p.m. until 3.30 p.m. on 12 October 2013.
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: The meeting to mark Coming Out Day was planned to be held at the Field of Mars (Марсово поле), a large square in the city centre of St Petersburg.
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: About 150 people were expected to attend the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: The organisers of the Coming Out Day meeting mentioned that some participants would arrive at 1.30 p.m. on 12 October 2013 to prepare for the meeting.
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: On 30 September 2013 the St Petersburg authorities forwarded information about the upcoming Coming Out Day meeting to the police (ГУ МВД Российской Федерации по г. Санкт-Петербургу и Ленинградской области).
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: On 30 September 2013 the St Petersburg authorities reminded the organisers of the Coming Out Day meeting that they would be held liable under domestic law for inciting hatred and enmity on account of ethnicity, language, origin and religious beliefs.
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: On 30 September 2013 the St Petersburg authorities reminded the organisers of the Coming Out Day meeting that they would be held liable under domestic law for promoting 'non-traditional' sexual relationships to minors.
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: The police deployed around 540 police officers, including officers from special-purpose units, to ensure public order during the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: The enhanced security deployment of approximately 540 police officers was ordered in the light of anticipated clashes with counter-demonstrators.
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: There is no information about any other prior arrangements made by the authorities in connection with the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
section_path: I. PUBLIC EVENT TO MARK COMING OUT DAY

text: At 11.30 a.m. on 12 October 2013 police officers arrived at the Field of Mars in St Petersburg.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: It does not appear that any crowd barriers were installed at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: It does not appear that the police erected any kind of perimeter fence for the demonstrators at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: At about 1 p.m. on 12 October 2013 the applicant arrived at the Field of Mars to take part in the preparation of the Coming Out Day meeting.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: According to the applicant, the Coming Out Day participants (about twenty or thirty people) were unable to gather at the Field of Mars because the place was blocked by more than 100 aggressive counter-demonstrators.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: According to the applicant, many of the counter-demonstrators were in national costumes and armed with whips (нагайка).
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: According to the applicant, the counter-demonstrators insulted the participants in the Coming Out Day meeting.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: According to the applicant, the counter-demonstrators pushed and punched the participants in the Coming Out Day meeting.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: According to the applicant, the counter-demonstrators surrounded the Coming Out Day participants, including the applicant, and followed them.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: According to the applicant, the Coming Out Day participants asked for help from the police officers present at the Field of Mars, but the police officers did not react.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: According to the applicant, the police officers at the Field of Mars stepped in only when counter-demonstrators insulted the police officers personally.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: According to the applicant, the police officers arrested several counter-demonstrators, took them to a police bus parked nearby, and then released them.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: According to the applicant, the released counter-demonstrators continued their verbal attacks and physical pressure on the LGBTI activists present at the Field of Mars.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: At 1.55 p.m. on 12 October 2013 police officers surrounded a group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, Mr D.G., Mr D.M., Ms N.I., Ms E.M., Ms S.L. and Ms Y.T.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: The police officers stated that the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, had breached public order by using foul language in a public place.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: The police officers ordered the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, to proceed to a police bus.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: The police officers took the group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, to central police station no. 28 in St Petersburg (28 отдел полиции УМВД России по центральному району г. Санкт-Петербургу).
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: The police officers referred to the transfer procedure set out in Article 27.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences as the legal basis for taking the demonstrators to central police station no. 28 in St Petersburg.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: The Government submitted that in total, ninety-three people had been arrested during the public event on 12 October 2013 on account of their disorderly conduct.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: The Government submitted that the ninety-three people arrested during the public event on 12 October 2013 were taken to three police stations and then released.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: The applicant argued that the police officers had taken only participants in the Coming Out Day meeting to various police stations on 12 October 2013.
section_path: II. THE APPLICANT'S ATTEMPT TO TAKE PART IN THE MEETING AND HER ARREST

text: The applicant was detained at central police station no. 28 in St Petersburg under Article 27.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences from 2.30 p.m. to around 6.30 p.m. on 12 October 2013.
section_path: III. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT

text: According to the applicant, at around 6 p.m. on 12 October 2013 police officers started drawing up administrative-arrest, administrative-escort and administrative-offence records.
section_path: III. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT

text: The administrative-arrest record stated that the applicant had been detained at 1.55 p.m. on 12 October 2013 on account of her disorderly conduct, an offence proscribed by Article 20.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
section_path: III. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT

text: The administrative-arrest record stated that the applicant had been taken to the police station to ensure the 'prompt and proper examination of her case'.
section_path: III. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT

text: The administrative-offence record specified that the grounds of the applicant's arrest were that she had used foul language during the public meeting and had ignored warnings given by police officers to refrain from doing so.
section_path: III. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT

text: The applicant signed the administrative-arrest record and the administrative-offence record, noting her disagreement with them.
section_path: III. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT

text: The applicant's administrative case was transmitted to the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg.
section_path: III. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT

text: The Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg terminated the administrative proceedings against the applicant on 8 November 2013 for lack of evidence of her guilt.
section_path: III. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT

text: The police brought charges of disorderly misconduct (use of foul language) against Mr D.G., Mr D.M., Ms N.I., Ms E.M., Ms S.L. and Ms Y.T.
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: The Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg terminated the administrative proceedings against Mr D.G. for lack of evidence of his guilt on a date in November or December 2013.
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: The Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg terminated the administrative proceedings against Mr D.M. for lack of evidence of his guilt on a date in November or December 2013.
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: The Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg terminated the administrative proceedings against Ms E.M. for lack of evidence of her guilt on a date in November or December 2013.
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: The Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg terminated the administrative proceedings against Ms S.L. for lack of evidence of her guilt on a date in November or December 2013.
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: The Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg terminated the administrative proceedings against Ms Y.T. for lack of evidence of her guilt on a date in November or December 2013.
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: On 9 January 2014 the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg found Ms N.I. guilty of disorderly misconduct (use of foul language).
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: Ms N.I. appealed against the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision of 9 January 2014 finding her guilty.
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: On 6 March 2014 the St Petersburg City Court quashed the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision of 9 January 2014 finding Ms N.I. guilty.
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: The St Petersburg City Court found on 6 March 2014 that the police had failed to substantiate the charges of disorderly misconduct against Ms N.I. and terminated the proceedings against her.
section_path: IV. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST OTHER PARTICIPANTS OF THE PUBLIC EVENT

text: On 12 February 2014 the applicant lodged a civil claim with the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg against the St Petersburg and Leningrad Region Main Department of the Russian Ministry of the Interior (Главное управление МВД России по г. Санкт-Петербургу и Ленинградской области).
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 12 February 2014 the applicant lodged a civil claim with the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg against the Central District of St Petersburg Department of the Russian Ministry of the Interior (УМВД России по Центральному району г. Санкт-Петербурга).
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 12 February 2014 the applicant lodged a civil claim with the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg against the chief of central police station no. 28 in St Petersburg.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 12 February 2014 the applicant lodged a civil claim with the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg against two police officers involved in her transfer to central police station no. 28 in St Petersburg and her detention there.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: In her civil claim of 12 February 2014, the applicant challenged the lawfulness of her arrest and detention at central police station no. 28 in St Petersburg.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On an unspecified date after 12 February 2014, the applicant extended her civil claim, alleging that the authorities had failed to ensure the personal safety of the participants in the public meeting of 12 October 2013.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 17 February 2014 the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg rejected the applicant's civil claim on procedural grounds, without examining it on the merits.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The applicant appealed against the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision of 17 February 2014 rejecting her civil claim on procedural grounds.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 14 July 2014 the St Petersburg City Court quashed the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision of 17 February 2014 rejecting the applicant's civil claim on procedural grounds.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 23 October 2014 the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg examined the merits of the applicant's civil claim and dismissed it.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg noted on 23 October 2014 that the applicant had failed to comply with the three-month statutory time-limit for appealing against the police's actions.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg stated on 23 October 2014 that the applicant's civil claim was in any event ill-founded.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: Relying on a video recording of the event of 12 October 2013, the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg established that the police had interfered with the public gathering because of the conflict between the demonstrators and counter-demonstrators.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg found on 23 October 2014 that the applicant had been one of the active participants in the conflict between demonstrators and counter-demonstrators on 12 October 2013.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg concluded on 23 October 2014 that the applicant's arrest had been lawful.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg was not convinced by witness evidence stating that the applicant herself had not breached public order, because the witnesses belonged to the same group of demonstrators as the applicant.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg concluded on 23 October 2014 that the applicant's detention had been lawful, as its duration had not exceeded forty-eight hours, the maximum length of administrative detention provided by Article 27.5 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg found on 23 October 2014 that the applicant's allegation regarding the authorities' failure to ensure the personal safety of the demonstrators had been unsubstantiated by evidence.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg noted on 23 October 2014 that about 550 police officers had been deployed by the authorities during the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg noted on 23 October 2014 that no harm had been caused to the applicant during the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 31 December 2014 the applicant appealed against the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg's judgment of 23 October 2014 to the St Petersburg City Court.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: In her appeal of 31 December 2014, the applicant complained that her arrest had not pursued a legitimate aim and had been arbitrary.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: In her appeal of 31 December 2014, the applicant alleged that the authorities had failed to comply with their positive obligations under the Convention.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: In her appeal of 31 December 2014, the applicant alleged that instead of ensuring the participants' freedom of expression, the police officers had arrested them.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: In her appeal of 31 December 2014, the applicant alleged that no counter-demonstrators had been detained during the Coming Out Day meeting on 12 October 2013.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: In her appeal of 31 December 2014, the applicant alleged that the selective approach of arresting only Coming Out Day participants and not counter-demonstrators had been discriminatory.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 11 March 2015 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg's judgment of 23 October 2014 on appeal.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The St Petersburg City Court concluded on 11 March 2015 that the applicant's arrest had been lawful.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The St Petersburg City Court considered on 11 March 2015 that the applicant's arrest was an interim measure taken to facilitate subsequent administrative proceedings for the use of foul language.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The St Petersburg City Court found on 11 March 2015 that at the time of the event, given the tension between the participants of the assembly and counter-demonstrators, the police officers had been unable to identify the people who had used offensive language and to immediately draft the administrative-offence records.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The St Petersburg City Court found on 11 March 2015 that the police officers had therefore had to take the arrested people to the police station.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The St Petersburg City Court found on 11 March 2015 that the fact that the administrative proceedings against the applicant had subsequently been terminated had not invalidated the lawfulness of her arrest.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: The St Petersburg City Court noted on 11 March 2015 that the applicant's civil claim had been lodged belatedly.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 2 September 2015 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal challenging the Vasileostrovskiy District Court of St Petersburg's judgment of 23 October 2014 and the St Petersburg City Court's appeal decision of 11 March 2015.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 25 September 2015 the St Petersburg City Court dismissed the applicant's cassation appeal, upholding the findings of the lower-instance courts.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On an unspecified date after 25 September 2015, the applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court of Russia challenging the lower courts' decisions.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: On 20 February 2016 the Supreme Court of Russia declined to entertain the applicant's cassation appeal.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: It appears that the applicant did not receive a written version of the Supreme Court of Russia's decision of 20 February 2016.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: Subsequently, the applicant requested the Supreme Court of Russia to provide her with a copy of its decision of 20 February 2016.
section_path: V. CIVIL PROCEEDINGS AGAINST POLICE AUTHORITIES

text: By a letter of 23 May 2019, the Supreme Court of Russia informed the applicant that the case file had been destroyed owing to the expiration of the statutory period for its storage.

On 31 March 2010, at the 1081st meeting of Ministers' Deputies, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe adopted Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 on measures to combat discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe provides that member states should take appropriate measures at national, regional and local levels to ensure that the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, as enshrined in Article 11 of the Convention, can be effectively enjoyed without discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe provides that member states should ensure that law enforcement authorities take appropriate measures to protect participants in peaceful demonstrations in favour of the human rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons from any attempts to unlawfully disrupt or inhibit the effective enjoyment of their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) were prepared by the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) in consultation with the European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission) of the Council of Europe.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that states have a positive duty to facilitate and protect the exercise of the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, which should be reflected in the legislative framework and relevant law enforcement regulations and practices.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that the duty to facilitate assemblies includes a duty to facilitate assemblies at the organiser's preferred location and within 'sight and sound' of the intended audience.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that the duty to protect involves the protection of assembly organizers and participants from third party individuals or groups who seek to undermine their right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that discrimination based on grounds such as sexual orientation, gender, and gender identity should be prohibited.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that law enforcement agencies should adopt a human rights-based approach to all aspects of the planning, preparation and policing of assemblies.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that a human rights-based approach to policing assemblies should be based on four key principles: (1) knowledge of the groups involved; (2) a commitment to facilitating assemblies; (3) recognition of the value and importance of voluntary communication at all stages of the assembly process; and (4) acknowledgment of the diversity of participants in assemblies and the need to differentiate between them in active policing.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that law enforcement agencies should not use force at assemblies unless strictly unavoidable, and that force should only be applied to the minimum extent necessary, following the principles of restraint, proportionality, and minimization of damage and the preservation of life.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that law enforcement should as far as possible avoid the use of containment or mass arrests of participants at an assembly, as such indiscriminate measures may amount to an arbitrary deprivation of liberty under international human rights law.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that state authorities must protect the organizers and participants of peaceful assemblies that espouse controversial or unpopular views from hostile opposition, and shall protect peaceful assemblies from any person or group that intentionally seeks to limit or destroy the rights of others to assemble.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that potential disorder arising from hostility directed against those participating in a peaceful assembly must not be used to justify disproportionate restrictions on the assembly.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that an assembly may be prohibited as a last resort measure when the risk of violent counter-demonstrations may not otherwise be prevented or mitigated, and that the principle of proportionality must always be respected.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that the state has the duty to ensure that counter-demonstrators do not constitute an undue and serious interference with the main event's ability to convey its message.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that the state should take positive measures to facilitate assemblies associated with individuals and groups that have historically faced discrimination, or are otherwise marginalized or at risk.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that law enforcement officials must differentiate between peaceful and non-peaceful participants, since only those who themselves take part in violence forfeit the legal guarantee of their right to assemble, and that state intervention should target individual wrongdoers rather than all participants more generally.

The 2019 Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (CDL-AD(2019)017) provide that if a dispute arises during the course of an assembly, communication between the organizer and the competent state authorities may be an appropriate means by which to reach an acceptable resolution, and that where voluntary dialogue is not possible, the relevant law enforcement bodies must still ensure that their actions are aimed at de-escalating tensions.

In a report entitled 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia' published in December 2014, the NGO Human Rights Watch stated that since at least the mid-2000s, Russian authorities had refused to tolerate most public events in support of LGBT rights and equality.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch stated that homophobic counter-demonstrators had violently disrupted many public events in support of LGBT rights and equality in Russia.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch stated that the vast majority of people it interviewed who had been involved in such events said that the frequency of attacks had risen over the previous two years.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch stated that in 2013 anti-gay activists had attacked virtually every LGBT equality event of which Human Rights Watch were aware.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch described how anti-gay counter-protesters routinely harassed LGBT activists and their supporters during public events, used offensive homophobic slurs, or threatened them with physical violence.

In the December 2014 report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', Human Rights Watch stated that in five out of seven cases documented in the report, police had not taken adequate measures to prevent and stop the harassment and attacks.

One of the five cases in which police had not taken adequate measures to prevent and stop harassment and attacks, as documented in the December 2014 Human Rights Watch report 'License to Harm: Violence and Harassment against LGBT People and Activists in Russia', concerned the public meeting of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.
A Human Rights Watch researcher observed the Coming Out Day rally organized by LGBT activists on 12 October 2013 at the Field of Mars in central St Petersburg.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, after about a dozen LGBT activists arrived at the Field of Mars for the Coming Out Day rally on 12 October 2013, a crowd of at least five times as many anti-gay counter-protesters harassed and attacked them.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, some of the counter-protesters at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 were dressed as priests with religious accessories; others were in military uniforms and camouflage outfits.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the counter-protesters at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 yelled that gays were 'abnormal' and that there was no place for them in St Petersburg, and blocked access for LGBT activists to the protest venue.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, after several attempts to reach the venue at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013, the LGBT activists were unable to start the Coming Out Day event.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the LGBT activists told the police at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 that they were effectively barred from reaching the event venue.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the police at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013, who numbered several dozen ordinary police officers and many riot police, did not take adequate measures to ensure access to the venue and prevent harassment and attacks by anti-gay counter-protesters.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the police at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 began detaining counter-protesters only when several of them started insulting police officers for not stopping the LGBT rally.
According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, a few LGBT activists were also detained at the Field of Mars on 12 October 2013 but were released after several hours.

According to the Human Rights Watch researcher's observations, the initial charges against the detained LGBT activists of organizing and participating in an unsanctioned public event were eventually dropped.
